### 5.1.2 Mapping injury-related deaths by stay-at-home orders & sex {#chloropethInjSex}

So, hopefully you've noticed what I've noticed about the relationship between the stay-at-home orders and the proportion of overall deaths due to accident or injury, as well as the effect of the shutdown in terms of both decedent biological sexes. You know from your earlier graph that females have a lower proportion of overall death due to accident or injury; next, it would be nice to see what the relationship is spatiotemporally (before and after shutdown) on average accident / injury mortality overall, as well as for each of the sexes separately. This will allow you to see if there is a geographic pattern, as one might expect in denser areas with more roadways, with the effect or not.

Let's add a label to the dataset to identify whether a month was under stay-at-home orders or not, and call the new feature `stayAtHome`. Notice that I could have coded it as a dummy variable (0 or 1) where 1 is the stay-at-home order condition, but instead I chose to encode it as a category. I can also change the encoding later, if needed. Note also that although I chose to use `Date` as the condition for my `ifelse()`, you could just as easily have chosen a joint conditional using both`Month` and `Year` columns!

```{r}
## Encode stayAtHome as any date after March 19, 2020
injDeaths <- injDeaths %>% 
  mutate(stayAtHome = ifelse(Date >= "2020-03-19", "Stay-at-Home", "None"))
```

Next, let's calculate a summarized dataframe that groups by `stayAtHome`, `Year`, and `County`, then summarizes an average `deathsInjuriesProportion` for use with the maps. Notice that rather than storing the summarized dataframe, I simply piped it through to join it with the geometry from the shapefile for map-making this time. I was feeling a bit lazy. 
```{r}
##### Calculate the proportion of all deaths due to injury
injuryDeathSummary <- injDeaths %>% 
  ## Group by stay-at-home order, year, county, AND sex
  group_by(stayAtHome, Year, County, biologicalSex) %>% 
  ## Change the name to make the join easier
  rename(COUNTY_NAM = County) %>% 
  ## Mean proportion of deaths for each month-year-county-sex combo
  summarise(deathsInjuriesPercent = mean(deathsInjuriesProportion, na.rm = TRUE)*100) %>% 
  ## Join to get the geometries for mapping
  full_join(cali_sf, by = "COUNTY_NAM", relationship = "many-to-many") %>% 
  ## Coerce to make sure it is seen as a shapefile
  st_as_sf() %>% 
  ungroup() 

#### Find the five number summary
summ <- fivenum(injuryDeathSummary$deathsInjuriesPercent)
paste0("The five-number summary of % of deaths that are accident/injury-related is: ")
paste(c("Min", "Lower Quartile", "Median", "Upper Quartile", "Max"), 
      round(summ, 3))
## Notice that, with the minimum, 1st quartile, AND median all equal to 0, we
## really only have three groups

##### Now add on the cuts injuryDeathSummary labels for mapping:
injuryDeathSummary <- injuryDeathSummary %>% 
  mutate(deathLabels = cut(deathsInjuriesPercent, 
                          breaks = c(0, 3.343, 18.489, Inf),
                          labels = c("0-3.342", "3.343-18.489", "18.489+"),
                          ordered_result = TRUE, right = F)) 
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
## Initialize the plot
ggplot(injuryDeathSummary) +
  ## Chloropeth: draw the polygons of the counties and color by total deaths
  geom_sf(aes(fill = deathLabels), color = "gray20", size = 0.2) +

  ## Apply manual fill scale for total deaths
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "% of Deaths Due to Accident or Injury",
    values = c4a(palette="brewer.or_rd", n=3),
    na.value = "gray70",
    drop = FALSE
  ) +
  ## Set map projection explicitly
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +   ## <- keeps map tight to its bounding box

  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),

    axis.ticks = element_blank(),

  # Add title and caption
  labs(
    title = "California Annual Percent Deaths due to Accident or Injury, by County",
    subtitle = "Cumulative Monthly Deaths, Jan 2017 - Aug 2020",
    caption = "Source: California DPH Vital Records"
  ) + 
  
  ## Use facet_wrap to make one map per year
  facet_wrap(~ Year, ncol = 4)
```

### 5.1.3 Controlling for population-level differences in sex ratio

Even if you didn't explore biological sex on the map, it seems that there are likely some sex-specific effects in percent of deaths due to accident and injury. But what if some counties have a **skewed sex ratio**? You might need to adjust for that! Although you might expect, _a priori_, for all counties to have a female to male ratio of 1:1, in reality that isn't always the case. 

In order to determine if you need to control for any underlying population-level differences in the sex ratio of each county, you make a simple histogram and plot a 1:1 line where the proportion of females in the population will equal males. You do this for each county. You make a **blue, solid line** for the mean sex-ratio, and a **black, dashed line** to show the reference 1:1 line. 

**Note** that this ratio is coming from the Census data that you imported earlier; you calculated this sex ratio in an earlier code chunk from those data. Thus, these data are from 2020.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
injDeaths %>% 
ggplot(aes(x = femaleMaleRatio)) +
  ## Make a histogram showing the female:male sex ratio
  geom_histogram(alpha = 0.7, fill = skittles[5], color = "white") +
  ## Add the mean as a solid, dark blue line
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(injDeaths$femaleMaleRatio)), 
             color = skittles[9], 
             linetype = "solid", 
             size = 1.25)+
  ## Add the reference 1:1 line as a black, dashed line
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 1), 
             color = "black", 
             linetype = "dashed", size = 1.25)+
  labs(title = "Female:Male adults in California counties",
       subtitle = "Solid, blue line is mean ratio; black, dashed line represents 1:1 reference",
       y = "Frequency", 
       x = "Adult Female:Male",
       caption = "Source: California Decennial Census, 2020") +
  theme_minimal()
```

You can see that you have a very strongly __left-skewed__ distribution, with the mean of the female:male ratio dragged to the left. What does this mean, exactly? **You have more counties with a higher proportion of men than women than otherwise!** And since men seem to have a higher proportion of deaths by accident / injury as opposed to females, you need to decide if you think you need to account for this in your maps. Accounting for it in the model will be easy - you just include the female:male ratio as a predictor variable. However, in the maps it is actually a little trickier and would require a mathematical correction that could be difficult for your stakeholders to understand. Is it even necessary then?

#### Question 22 [1 point]:

Calculate the correlation of `femaleMaleRatio` and the `deathsInjuriesProportion`, making sure to be careful to drop or exclude any NAs before making your calculation. 

```{r}
# Pearson correlation, dropping any row with NA in either variable
cor(injDeaths$femaleMaleRatio,
    injDeaths$deathsInjuriesProportion,
    use = "complete.obs")

injClean <- injDeaths %>%
  filter(!is.na(femaleMaleRatio), !is.na(deathsInjuriesProportion))

cor.test(injClean$femaleMaleRatio, injClean$deathsInjuriesProportion)

```

Do you think that this correlation coefficient indicates that you need to make a correction on your maps, or is it likely sufficient just to make the correction in your models? In other words, large correlation coefficients (in the absolute value sense) would indicate a need to correct the maps; smaller coefficients would indicate that it's probably not a big deal for your visualizations provided to stakeholders.

**Answer:**
No, a correlation of 0.28 is small enough that I don't think the maps need a correction. it's a weak relationship: the female:male ratio accounts for only about 8% of the variation in the injury-death proportion (0.28² ≈ 0.08), so adjusting every county's map value for its sex ratio would shuffle the shading only slightly while adding a mathematical step my stakeholders would find hard to follow. The p-value is tiny, but that's just the large sample size talking, with ~1,870 rows almost any non-zero correlation turns up "significant," so the effect size, not the p-value, is what should drive this call. So I'll handle the sex ratio where it's cheap and transparent. as a predictor in the model and leave the maps as straightforward, uncorrected proportions, noting the caveat in plain language rather than baking in a correction.


#### Question 23 [1 point]:

Now, take a look at the scatter plot below with a best-fit line. Does the plot agree with the correlation coefficient (i.e., direction of slope) you obtained? Why or why not?

```{r, echo = FALSE}
injDeaths %>% 
  group_by(County) %>%
  summarise(femaleMaleRatio = mean(femaleMaleRatio),
            deathsInjuriesPercent = mean(deathsInjuriesProportion, 
                                         na.rm = TRUE)*100) %>% 

  ggplot(aes(x = femaleMaleRatio, y = deathsInjuriesPercent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, color = skittles[5]) +
  geom_smooth(color = skittles[8], method = "lm") +
  labs(title = "Accident-related Deaths vs. Female:Male Adults in California counties",
       subtitle = "Each point represents a county average",
       y = "Average % of Total Deaths Due to Injury or Accident", 
       x = "Adult Female:Male (California Decennial Census, 2020)",
       caption = "Source: California DPH Vital Records") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Answer:**
Yes,agrees. The best-fit line slopes upward,positive. which matches the positive correlation of 0.28 I calculated. That agreement isn't a coincidence: the slope of a simple best-fit line and the sign of a Pearson correlation are always the same thing, because the slope equals r times the ratio of the two standard deviations (slope = r · s_y/s_x), and standard deviations are always positive. So a positive correlation must produce an upward-sloping line， they're just two ways of expressing the same linear relationship.

#### Question 24 [3 points]:
Originally, I was going to walk you through predictive modeling here as well - but given a need to abbreviate this project, instead I am going to ask you to simply construct **data science question** and **hypothesis** given the information you have here so far. Are there any variables you pulled from the Census that would be worth considering here as well?

Choose what kind of model you would do. Would you include spatial lags? Ideally, would you include temporal lags?

**Answer:**

1. Data science question: Is a county's sex composition (its female-to-male ratio) a meaningful predictor of the proportion of deaths due to injury or accident, after accounting for spatial structure, temporal structure, and the county's age profile?
2. Hypothesis: A county's female-to-male ratio is associated with its injury/accident death proportion, but based on the weak bivariate correlation I found earlier (r = 0.28, and in the opposite direction from the demographic intuition), I expect any effect to be small, and quite possibly to weaken or disappear once age structure and spatial/temporal autocorrelation are accounted for. So I'm really testing not just whether sex ratio is a significant predictor (with this many observations, almost anything is) but whether it's a meaningful one.
3. Model: I would include spatial lags, definitely. The counties are largely arbitrary boundaries, so include some info between neighbors through a spatial lag should better capture the actual spatial trends. I'd try multiple models, starting with a SAR model and then exploring an SEM if the diagnostics point to spatial error rather than a spatial lag. I would also include temporal lags: in the earlier random-forest work, recent mortality was the single strongest predictor, so a county's recent injury history likely carries real month-to-month momentum though I'd watch that the lags don't absorb the very signal I'm trying to measure. Beyond that, I'd add more demographic predictors from the Census (age structure, especially % over 65, is the strongest one I already have; true socioeconomic variables like income or education would need an additional Census pull). Increasing the complexity that way would also let me try a decision-tree model like Random Forest and see how it compares with the added benefit that its variable-importance metrics could shed light directly on where sex ratio ranks against the other predictors.

```{r}
## Pull just the PNF rows and collapse the two sex rows into one count per county-month
pnfDeaths <- sexDeaths %>% 
  full_join(census, by = "County") %>%

  filter(leadingCauseDeath == "PNF") %>%

         ## The ratio of females to males in the population

         ## Ratio of retirees to non-retirees
         retireeRatio = over65/totalN,

                        format = "%Y-%m-%d")) %>%

  mutate(deathsPnfProportion = ifelse(deathsPnfProportion == "NaN",  0, deathsPnfProportion))

## ---- sanity checks ----
```

1. **Annual chloropeth maps showing your cause-of-death**, like this [one](#chloropethInjSex)
```{r}
## A. collapse sex-split rows to one clean row per county-month
pnfMonthly <- pnfDeaths %>%
  group_by(County, Year, Month) %>%
  summarise(pnfDeaths   = sum(pneumoniaDeaths, na.rm = TRUE),  # over both sexes
            totalDeaths = first(totalDeaths),                     # both-sex total (don't double-count)
            .groups = "drop")

## B. aggregate to county-YEAR and compute the annual %
pnfAnnual <- pnfMonthly %>%
  group_by(County, Year) %>%
  summarise(pnfDeaths   = sum(pnfDeaths,   na.rm = TRUE),
            totalDeaths = sum(totalDeaths, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(deathsPnfPercent = ifelse(totalDeaths > 0, pnfDeaths / totalDeaths * 100, NA_real_)) %>%
  rename(COUNTY_NAM = County)

## C. bin the continuous % into map categories
summ <- fivenum(pnfAnnual$deathsPnfPercent)
paste(c("Min","Lower Quartile","Median","Upper Quartile","Max"), round(summ, 3))
pnfAnnual <- pnfAnnual %>%
  mutate(deathLabels = cut(deathsPnfPercent,
                           breaks = c(-Inf, 0, 0.5, 1, 2, Inf),
                           labels = c("0", "0-0.5", "0.5-1", "1-2", "2+"),
                           include.lowest = TRUE))

## D. attach the county polygons
caliGeo     <- cali_sf %>% distinct(COUNTY_NAM, .keep_all = TRUE)
pnfAnnualSf <- pnfAnnual %>%
  full_join(caliGeo, by = "COUNTY_NAM", relationship = "many-to-many") %>%
  st_as_sf()

## E. draw one map per year
ggplot(pnfAnnualSf) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = deathLabels), color = "gray20", size = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(name = "% of Deaths Due to Pneumonia or Influenza",
                    values = c4a(palette = "brewer.or_rd", n = 5),
                    na.value = "gray70", drop = FALSE) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(), axis.title = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(title = "California Annual Percent Deaths due to Pneumonia or Influenza, by County",
       subtitle = "Cumulative Monthly Deaths, Jan 2017 - Aug 2020",
       caption = "Source: California DPH Vital Records") +
  facet_wrap(~ Year, ncol = 4)
```

4. **Interpretation** of all graphs or analyses explored.

**Answer:**
What I could learn from all graphs for now, pneumonia makes up a bigger slice of deaths in the larger southern and inland counties: San Bernardino, Riverside, Imperial, and a band through the Central Valley and the pattern stays pretty stable year to year.The grey and cream counties up north aren't pneumonia-free; they're just small enough that the monthly, sex-split counts get suppressed for privacy and come through as zero. So the maps are really only telling me about the bigger counties. There's a little bump in 2020, San Bernardino slides into the darkest bin,  but flu seasons bounce around from year to year anyway, so I wouldn't lean on that too hard.

The line graph is where the COVID story falls apart to me.  Summing all the counties together by month gives a clean seasonal wave: pneumonia peaks every winter and drops off in summer, and the rough 2017–18 flu season sticks out as the tallest January. But 2020 doesn't spike. It rides along with the other years in winter and then sits near the bottom through spring and summer. That threw me until I remembered that COVID deaths got their own code (U07.1), so they never landed in the pneumonia bucket, and on top of that, COVID drove total deaths way up, and that's the denominator. So pneumonia's share of deaths goes down in 2020 even though more people were dying. The pandemic shows up here as a dip, not a spike, which is the opposite of what we'd guess.

The scatter tell another different story to me. Older counties have a lower pneumonia share, not higher, the correlation came out negative (−0.47), backwards from everything we know about pneumonia hitting the elderly hardest. Digging in, two things were going on. The obvious one is suppression again: the oldest counties are the small rural retirement ones (Amador, Calaveras, that crowd), and they're suppressed to zero. But even after I narrowed it to just the big counties, the negative stuck around (−0.38), so it's not only an artifact. The counties carrying the high pneumonia share are the younger, bigger, inland ones, and that probably has more to do with air quality, income, and healthcare access out there than with age, though those are things I'd want to test, not just assert. It's a clean case of the ecological fallacy: pneumonia really does hit older people harder, but older counties don't have higher pneumonia shares, because at the county level you're looking at the whole mix of deaths, not individual risk.
Put together, the three pieces say the same thing: the share of deaths from pneumonia isn't driven by the obvious suspects, the pandemic, or how old the county is,  so much as by how the data get coded and suppressed, and by what kind of county you're looking at. The one thing that's solid and survives all of it is the seasonality.

5. **A data science question you would like to test**

**Answer:**
Does a California county's over-65 share genuinely predict its pneumonia/influenza death proportion, or does that association disappear once I control for population size and for the socioeconomic, healthcare-access, and air-quality differences that distinguish younger inland counties from older coastal ones?

6. **A data science hypothesis based on what you found** [Note: if you find nothing compelling, you may defend with evidence why there is no point developing a hypothesis instead.]

**Answer:**
My hypothesis is that a county's age structure isn't really what drives pneumonia's share of deaths. I think the negative correlation I found is mostly a product of suppression and confounding rather than a true effect of age. If I controlled for population size, I'd expect the association to drop sharply, because the small, old counties that get suppressed to zero are what pull it most negative to begin with. Once I brought in the kinds of variables that set younger inland counties apart, like socioeconomic status, healthcare access, and air quality, I'd expect whatever negative is left to shrink toward zero or stop being significant. So my prediction is that the share of residents over 65 ends up a weak or insignificant predictor once those variables are in the model, and certainly not the positive predictor you'd expect from how hard pneumonia hits the elderly. If anything still predicts pneumonia's share, my money is on the type of county itself, meaning the younger, lower income, inland counties that seem to carry more of it, rather than age.
Two outcomes would prove me wrong. If the share of residents over 65 stayed strongly negative even after all of those controls, I'd have to treat it as a real county effect rather than an artifact. And if it flipped positive once the confounders were in, that would tell me those variables had been hiding the individual risk all along.
